vintage Soviet synthesizers, field recordings, and hypnotic percussion, x.y.r. builds an ambient universe that feels both ancient and futuristic.","full_text":"It’s rare when an artist’s name also feels like their mission statement. x.y.r. is the moniker of Russian producer Vladimir Karpov. The project’s name is an abbreviation for Xram Yedinennogo Razmuwlenuja, roughly translating to “Temple of Solitary Reflection.” Karpov’s music feels exactly like that. More than albums, it feels like he’s been creating a setting. Each x.y.r. album feels like a destination for listeners to bring themselves into, to clear their minds, and seek insights from within.

On x.y.r.’s latest album, “Saga”, that feeling of a physical space has never felt more tangible. Where ambient is often seen as spacious, Karpov grounds the music to earth with nature sounds and steady percussion loops. It’s an earthly foundation that serves as the base for Karpov’s otherworldly drones and synthesizer warps, utilizing what’s become his signature instrument—a Soviet-era synthesizer called the Formanta-Mini. The synthesizer and the loops create a sound that feels like a vision of the future from the vantage point of a bygone era.

Each of “Saga”’s four songs clocks in at around 20 minutes, each taking up a side of vinyl. But no song overstays its welcome. It’s just the right amount of time to completely envelop the listener in each of the worlds Karpov is creating. “Moonlight Raga” opens the record with the image of an endless horizon. You can practically hear the ground crunching beneath your feet alongside the chirping birds and crashing waves. Synthesizer notes whoosh by like the wind, echoing out until they finally decay in the distance. “Mysterious Cave” emulates the feeling of water dripping from the cavern ceilings, the hollow echoes of sound bouncing against the rocks. Moments like these are where his use of drums is especially effective—pounding and clanging in the distance, but also never overwhelming the atmosphere he’s creating.

“Saga” excels in the way that the best ambient music does, by touching on the infinite with expansive drones and capturing an innate peaceful feeling. But there’s something more happening with “Saga”. There’s an ominous, foreboding tone lingering underneath. As soothing as the music can be, it can also feel like there’s something lurking just out of view—a general uneasiness that’s felt but never seen. Even its dreamiest tracks, like “Etherealm,” have a feeling of uncertainty, a looming darkness hiding in otherwise gentle, soothing tones. Closer “Elysium” draws the album to a triumphant close, passing through dark clouds and black skies before it finally breaks through to the light at the end.

“Saga” is all about finding peace within the darkness—something Karpov has continually excelled at as x.y.r. He’s designing his own worlds and, just like our own, they’re imperfect and at times uneasy. “Saga” is a reminder that to best see the light, you need the shadow of darkness. Sometimes the most interesting parts can be found hiding in those shadows.
